body:
Shadow:

I've got to admit I let myself be influenced by other facts besides
the contents of TK's 1971 essay when I chose the phrase "envy and
hatred" rather than a milder term such as "dislike."  I don't think
I'll be able to convince you but since it's the psychological aspects
of the case that interest me most, I'd like to give it a try.

I (David Buchanan) wrote:
> So the goal of the Essay was to eliminate the prestige,
> the funding, and the jobs of all scientific
> researchers.  Consider the Essay's author.  In 1971, TK
> was a failed scientific researcher who knew he didn't
> have what it takes to succeed and who had no real
> future ahead of him.  The pattern is clear.  Envy and
> hatred of others is what drives him. Reducing everyone
> else to his level is the unstated goal of both the
> Manifesto and the Essay.

Shadow <shadow42@erols.com> wrote:
:Another interpretation is that TK, who had previously devoted his
:whole life to Science, realized the uses to which research could be
:put and foresaw future evils brought about by research that looked
:"harmless" today. And perhaps that is why he dropped out of the
:academic life, became a hermit, etc.

This is certainly one possible interpretation and the one TK wants us
to believe. Except perhaps for a few passing doubts, it's probably
what TK believes himself but that's always the way with
rationalizations and all of us rationalize our actions far more often
than we'd like to admit.  I suspect TK had a far greater need for
rationalizations than most of us do.

Manifesto, Paragraph # 26. 
"...Thus the oversocialized person is kept on a psychological
leash and spends his life running on rails that society has laid down
for him. In many oversocialized people this results in a sense of
constraint and powerlessness that can be a severe hardship. We suggest
that oversocialization is among the more serious cruelties that human
beings inflict on one another."
   
Oversocialization and the constraints it imposes on the oversocialized
person was one of the Unabomber's major complaints against
technological society.  So much space is devoted to it and "Feelings
of Inferiority" that it is hard to believe the Unabomber isn't voicing
a very personal complaint and sees himself as oversocialized and
constrained by a "psychological leash."  Even more than most people,
such a person would have a great need to rationalize his lethal
behavior, even to himself.

Step back a moment and consider it in a different context.  Suppose we
came across an essay advocating the abolition of all professional
sport written by a would-be professional football player whom we knew
had recently been washed out of training camp and had no future
prospects.   Most people would say the most likely reason the player's
essay was written was out of jealousy in an attempt to deny to others
what the player had been unable to obtain.  This is not to say, the
player's reasoning in the essay was right or wrong -- just that the
motive was probably not benevolent concern for others.

Shadow <shadow42@erols.com> wrote:
"Hatred of others"? I see very little of that. I don't see any
bromides directed at "evil researchers" per se. (I read the Nazi web
pages, I know what 'hatred' looks like.) I simply see a person who saw
through the Gods of our age (science and technology) and is making a
sincere (though hopeless) attempt to steer society away from this
"religion".

Here is where I was influenced by facts other than the contents of the
Essay.  Without the string of bombings and three murders, I'd probably
used a somewhat milder term than "hatred" but I believe it correctly
describes the Unabomber's attitude towards his victims.

From the April 24, 1995 letter to David Gelernter:
"People with advanced degrees aren't as smart as they think they are. 
If you'd had any brains you would have realized that there were a lot
of people out there who resent bitterly the way techno-nerds like you
are changing the world and you wouldn't have been dumb enough to open
an unexpected package from an unexpected source."
 
Directed to a man the Unabomber had already crippled of life, this
letter still reeks of personal hatred towards his victim.  Even after
crippling him, the Unabomber still needs to try to prove he's smarter
than Gelernter -- the techno-nerd who's "changing the world" and not
coincidentally, has the prestige and professional success that
accompanies it. 

I (David Buchanan) wrote:
> DISTURBED BY SEXUAL REFERENCES
> The author's well-known spelling ability deserts him at
> one place in the Essay.
> 
> Paragraph #19
> '.... Think of all the misery suffered as a result of
> Victorian repressions, sexual perversions, frigidity,
> unwanted pregnancies, and venerial desease
> [misspellings in original].  
> 
> "Venerial" and "desease" appear to be the only two
> misspelling in the entire Essay and although a
> mathematician might be forgiven for the first, the
> second is surprising.  It appears that something about
> the sexual references in first part of the sentence
> triggered an emotional reaction strong enough to
> interfere with the author's usually precise spelling.
> 
> I don't think one can infer much more from this other
> than that TK found sexual topics disturbing.


Shadow <shadow42@erols.com> wrote:
YES, DOCTOR FREUD!! :) :)

Please!  Anything but a Freudian.  A Freudian would have built an
entire psychoanalytical house of cards on those two misspelled words. 
Actually, I think Freud and the Freudians retarded the development of
psychology by at least 40 years.  Thankfully, the Freudians are pretty
well extinct -- at least outside of Departments of History and English
Literature where they continue to eke out a living finding hidden
sexual meanings in the placement of commas and semi-colons.  :-) 

Those two misspelled words don't tell us much but they do tell us that
TK was probably upset or rattled when he wrote them.  Emotional
reactions tend to interfere with tasks requiring control and
precision.  For example, if you can manage to get your golfing
opponent angry just before he takes his putt, you increase the chances
he will miss it.  Exactly what caused the emotional reaction in the
Essay, we can only guess but the sexual references preceding the
misspellings seem to be the most likely cause.  Of course, he could
have also been disturbed by something like a ringing telephone at that
point and not bothered to proof-read the document afterwards.

Try this one yourself.  Does the last half of Paragraph #51 of the
Essay seem as if TK was rattled or experiencing some sort of emotional
conflict when he wrote it?

Essay Paragraph #51
"I propose that you join me and a few other people to whom I am
writing in an attempt to found an organization dedicated to stopping
federal aid to scientific research.  I realize that you will probably
reject this suggestion, but I hope that you will not reject it on the
basis of some vague dogma such as "knowledge is good" READ the hope of 
READ.  Okay, knowledge is good, but how high a price, in terms of
freedom, are we going to pay for knowledge?  You may be understandably
reluctant to join an organization about which you know nothing, but
you know as much about it as I do.  It hasn't been started yet.  You
would be one of the founding members.  I claim to have no particular
qualifications for trying to start such an organization, and I have no
idea how to go about it, I am only making an attempt because no better
qualified person has yet done so.  I am simply trying to bring
together a few highly intelligent and thoughtful people who would be
willing to take over the task.  I would prefer to drop out of it
personally because I am unsuited to that kind of work:  in fact I
dislike it intensely.  "

[Readers can find the full text of the 1971 Essay and the Manifesto 
at "http://www.cs.umass.edu/~ehaugsja/unabom"  or
"http://www.redacted.com/" as well as other Unabomber information.]


--

headers.Subject: Re: Comments on Ted Kaczynski's 1971 Essay
